# Commercial KPIs a Board Will Trust

Source: https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Boards discount commercial numbers because definitions drift, sources disagree and forecasts miss. Gartner found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers have high confidence in their forecast accuracy. A trusted KPI passes four tests: one written definition, a reconciliation to the financials, a stable history with restatements recorded, and a named owner. This piece sets out the tests, an eight-measure pack and how to change a definition without losing the board.

A board trusts a commercial KPI when it has one written definition, reconciles to a number finance already reports, keeps the same meaning from quarter to quarter, and has a named owner who can explain a movement. Most commercial packs fail at least one of those tests. Gartner found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers have high confidence in their organisation's forecasting accuracy, and only 47% believe their organisation has high-quality data. The fix is not more metrics. It is fewer, defined once, with every change of definition recorded like any other commercial decision.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 6 set out the commercial operating rhythm: what gets reviewed weekly, monthly and quarterly. This part covers the numbers that rhythm produces once they leave the building. A sales team can live with rough figures in its own pipeline review, because the people in the room know the caveats. A board cannot. It sees the number without the caveats, compares it with last quarter's, and draws conclusions about strategy, hiring and cash.

## Why boards discount commercial numbers

Finance numbers arrive with a reconciliation and an audit trail. Commercial numbers usually arrive with neither. Three failures account for most of the distrust.

**Definitions drift.** "Qualified pipeline" means one thing in January and another in June, because a new sales leader tightened the stage criteria or marketing started counting webinar sign-ups. Nobody restates the history, so the trend line is two different measures joined together. Our explainer on [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) covers why stage exit criteria have to be written down for this reason alone.

**Sources disagree.** Marketing reports sourced pipeline from the automation platform, sales reports it from the CRM, and finance reports bookings from the billing system. The three rarely add up, and the board learns to trust none of them. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete, and 37% reported revenue lost as a direct result of poor data.

**Forecasts miss without explanation.** A missed forecast is survivable. A missed forecast with no account of why is not. Gartner's survey of 303 sales leaders, reported in February 2024, found 84% said sales analytics had influenced sales performance less than they expected, with poor data quality cited by 44% as a top barrier.

The common thread is that commercial numbers are produced by the people being measured, from systems that were configured for selling rather than reporting. That is not a reason to distrust the people. It is a reason to put the same controls around commercial numbers that finance already puts around its own.

## Four tests a trusted KPI passes

Finance teams already know how to make an adjusted measure credible: define it, reconcile it to the audited figure, and explain any change in how it is calculated. The standard setters say so. The SEC's 2020 guidance on metrics in MD&A expects a clear definition, how the metric is calculated, why it is useful and how management uses it, and notes that effective controls matter when such metrics are material. IFRS 18, effective from 1 January 2027, requires a note for management-defined performance measures that reconciles each one to an IFRS subtotal and explains how it is calculated and any changes to it. Commercial KPIs need the same treatment, expressed as four tests.

| Test | What it means | The failure it prevents | How to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defined once | One written definition, including inclusions, exclusions and the system of record | Two teams reporting the same name for different numbers | Ask two people to calculate it independently |
| Reconciled | The figure ties to something finance reports, or the gap is explained | Pipeline and bookings that never meet revenue | A reconciliation line in the appendix each quarter |
| Stable | The definition has not changed, or history has been restated | A trend that is really two measures stitched together | A change log with dates and the restated series |
| Owned | A named person explains movements and answers for the data | Numbers nobody can defend under questioning | The owner's name printed next to the measure |

The tests are deliberately boring. None requires new software. Each requires someone to write something down and keep it current, which is why they are skipped.

The a16z guide to startup metrics shows how often the first test fails in practice. It warns that bookings and revenue are not interchangeable, that annual recurring revenue should exclude one-time and professional service fees, and that blended customer acquisition cost can hide whether paid campaigns are profitable. Each is a definitional choice a board needs to see stated, because each can move the headline number without anything changing in the business.

## The eight measures that hold up

Most 20 to 500 person B2B firms can run a board pack on eight commercial measures. Services firms will substitute backlog and utilisation for some of the recurring-revenue measures; the tests stay the same.

| Measure | Question it answers | Reconciles to | Typical owner | Leading or lagging |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New bookings | How much new committed value did we sign? | Contract values; revenue as delivered | Head of sales | Lagging |
| Net revenue retention | Did existing customers grow, net of losses? | Recurring revenue by cohort | Head of account management | Lagging |
| Gross revenue retention | How much did we keep before expansion? | Recurring revenue by cohort | Head of account management | Lagging |
| Pipeline coverage | Is there enough qualified pipeline for the target? | Win rate and cycle length | Head of revenue operations | Leading |
| Win rate by segment | Are we winning where we chose to compete? | Closed-won and closed-lost records | Head of sales | Lagging |
| Sales cycle length | How long does a qualified deal take? | Stage dates in the CRM | Head of revenue operations | Leading |
| CAC payback | How long to recover the cost of winning a customer? | Sales and marketing spend; gross margin | Finance director | Lagging |
| Forecast accuracy | How close was the forecast to what landed? | Bookings | Head of sales | Both |

Three of these need particular care.

**Net revenue retention** blends expansion with churn. The a16z guide notes that net revenue churn "understates the losses" because upsells offset them, which is why gross retention sits beside it. For reference, SaaS Capital's 2025 survey of private B2B SaaS companies put median net revenue retention at 102% for firms with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000. A board seeing 102% should know whether that is healthy expansion over heavy churn or flat accounts with little of either.

**Pipeline coverage** is the most quoted and least understood. Salesforce's own guidance points out that the common "three times quota" rule holds only when the win rate is 33% and the sales cycle is one year; a seller winning 10% of pipeline revenue needs about ten times coverage. Report coverage alongside the win rate and cycle length that make it meaningful, or the board will apply the rule of thumb to a business it does not fit.

**Forecast accuracy** is the measure that most directly earns or loses trust. Report the forecast made at the start of the quarter, the forecast at mid-quarter and the outcome, every quarter, for eight quarters. A forecast that is consistently 10% optimistic is more useful to a board than one that is right on average and wildly wrong in either direction. Our piece on [calibration](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) sets out why the pattern of misses matters more than any single miss.

> A board will forgive a missed number. It will not forgive a number that changed meaning without anyone saying so.

## Define once, in one place

The practical form of the first test is a metric dictionary: one document or table listing each measure, its formula, its inclusions and exclusions, its system of record, its owner and the date it was last changed. It does not need special tooling. A shared document with version history is enough for a firm of 50.

Larger firms, or those already running a data warehouse, can put the definitions into code. The dbt documentation describes MetricFlow as a way to define each metric once, centrally, so that analysts do not each write their own version, noting that ad hoc queries "can lead to confusion, inconsistencies, and a headache for data management." Our explainer on [semantic layers](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) covers this pattern. The principle is the same at any size: the definition lives in one place, and every report reads from it.

The harder work is agreement. McKinsey's 2021 survey of more than 2,500 B2B respondents found that companies using commercial analytics effectively were 1.5 times more likely to achieve above-average growth, and that the first behaviour separating them was building cross-functional consensus on where analytics would create value. For KPIs, consensus means sales, marketing and finance signing the dictionary before it reaches the board. Gartner's 2024 finding points the same way: analytics led by the chief sales officer were 2.3 times more likely to achieve higher forecast accuracy, which suggests ownership matters as much as method.

None of this works on a CRM that cannot be trusted. Stage dates, close dates and amounts have to be maintained as a discipline, not cleaned up the week before the board meeting. Our explainer on [CRM data hygiene](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/) covers the routine.

## Changing a definition without losing the board

Definitions should change when the business changes. A firm that moves upmarket will tighten qualification; a firm that adds a partner channel will need to decide how partner-sourced pipeline is counted. The problem is never the change. It is the change made quietly.

The SEC's guidance sets a useful standard for any audience: when a metric's calculation changes, disclose how it differs from prior periods, why it changed and the effect on the reported figures, and consider whether to recast prior periods.

Treat a definition change as a commercial decision and record it the way Part 9 of The Build Order recommends for any decision worth recording: the decision, the reason, the owner, the status, the expected effect on the reported number, and a check date. Then do three things.

1. **Restate history.** Recalculate at least four prior quarters on the new definition, so the trend line compares like with like. If the old data cannot support the new definition, say so and show both series for a transition period.
2. **Tell the board first.** Flag the change in the pack before the number moves, with the size of the effect. A two-line note in the appendix is enough.
3. **Keep the old version.** The superseded definition stays in the dictionary, marked as replaced, with the date. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why the history of a definition is evidence in its own right.

The same discipline applies to targets. A target revised mid-year is a decision with a reason, and the board should see the original target, the revision and why.

## What the board pack looks like

The pack itself should be short. One page of commercial measures, with eight quarters of trend for each, the owner's name beside each line, and two or three sentences of commentary that name decisions rather than describe movements. "Win rate in the mid-market segment fell from 24% to 19% after we raised list prices; we are holding price and will review at the end of next quarter" is commentary. "Win rate decreased this quarter" is not.

Behind the page sits an appendix: the metric dictionary, the change log, and a reconciliation of bookings to recognised revenue. Most board members will never read it. The ones who do are the ones whose trust matters most.

Leave out what the board cannot act on. Our piece [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) argues the same point for early-stage firms: impressions, follower counts and raw lead volumes belong in the marketing team's own review, not in the pack.

Illustrative example: the pipeline restatement

Decision
:   Redefine qualified pipeline to require a confirmed budget holder and a dated next step, and restate the previous four quarters on the new basis.

Reason and owner
:   Marketing-sourced and sales-reported pipeline differed by more than a third, and the board had stopped referring to either. Owned by the head of revenue operations; definition signed by the heads of sales and marketing and the finance director.

What changed
:   Reported pipeline fell by roughly a quarter on restatement, coverage was reported with its win rate for the first time, and the board's questions moved from whether the number was real to whether it was enough.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements; figures are illustrative.

## lowob takeaways

- **Fewer measures, defined once.** Eight well-defined KPIs beat thirty that nobody can calculate twice.
- **Reconcile to finance.** Every commercial number should tie to something finance reports, or the gap should be explained.
- **Quote coverage with its assumptions.** Pipeline coverage means nothing without the win rate and cycle length behind it.
- **Record definition changes as decisions.** Restate history, tell the board first, keep the old version.
- **Name an owner on the page.** A number with a name beside it gets defended and maintained.

Gateway card

### Before the next board pack

- A metric dictionary covering every commercial measure in the pack
- Each measure signed off by sales, marketing and finance
- Bookings reconciled to recognised revenue in an appendix
- Pipeline coverage shown with its win rate and cycle length
- Forecast accuracy shown for at least four quarters
- A change log listing every definition change in the last year, with restated history
